summary: Diodorus (1st century BCE) on the "Atlantians" of north-west Africa: a people on the ocean shore with their own myths of the gods. A different, mythical Atlas from Plato's Atlantis, but one that later writers drew on.

tree.title: Diodorus Siculus 3.53-3.55: the Amazons of western Libya
tree.summary: Diodorus reports a tradition of a people on the western edge of Libya ruled by women, who serve as soldiers. Their queen Myrina leads them against the Atlantians, the Gorgons and others, near Lake Tritonis. He gives it as a story told, not as his own finding.

tree.title: Diodorus Siculus 3.56-3.57: the Atlantians and their myth of the gods
tree.summary: Diodorus describes the Atlantians as a pious, hospitable people on the shore of the ocean, who say the gods were born among them. Their first king Uranus civilised them and ruled the west and north. His forty-five sons include the Titans.

tree.title: Diodorus Siculus 3.58-3.59: the Great Mother and the story of Attis
tree.summary: A Phrygian variant of the myth of the Great Mother (Cybele): the foundling Cybele, her lover Attis and the king Meion's anger. The passage is background to the Titans story and has no direct bearing on Atlantis.

tree.title: Diodorus Siculus 3.60: Atlas, Hesperus and the Atlantides
tree.summary: Atlas, a son of Uranus, takes the coast of the ocean, and the Atlantians and Mount Atlas are named for him. He is credited with the doctrine of the sphere. His son Hesperus is snatched away on the mountain and honoured as a star. His daughters, the Atlantides, bear many heroes and become the Pleiades.

tree.title: Diodorus Siculus 3.61: Cronus, Zeus and the end of the Titans
tree.summary: Cronus marries Rhea and has Zeus the Olympian, who is distinguished from an earlier Cretan Zeus. The later Zeus becomes lord of the whole world. Diodorus closes his summary of what the Atlantians teach about the gods.
